pages.hook: At a farmers market in San Diego, fruit is sold by the pound or by the box, and the seller often says “That’s eleven dollars.” Learn to buy fruit like a local.

mythfact.s: In the USA, fruit is often sold by the pound.
mythfact.why: The pound (lb) is the common unit for weight in the USA.

mythfact.s: One pound is exactly one kilogram.
mythfact.why: One pound is about 0.45 kilograms, so a kilo is more than two pounds.

mythfact.s: A dozen means twelve.
mythfact.why: You can buy a dozen eggs or a dozen oranges.

mythfact.s: San Diego is in California.
mythfact.why: It is a coastal city in southern California.

mythfact.s: “Old Mother Hubbard” is an English nursery rhyme about a woman and her dog.
mythfact.why: In the rhyme, she goes to the cupboard to get a bone for her dog, but the cupboard is bare.

decode.q: How much are 3 pounds of apples?

compare.br: In Brazil, fruit at the feira is sold by the kilo, or by unit or dozen, like the dúzia of bananas or oranges.
compare.us: In the USA, you often hear “a pound of”, “a box of” or “a dozen”, and the sign shows the price per pound.
compare.tip: Remember: one pound is a little less than half a kilo.
compare.ask: What fruit do you buy? Say it in English.

quiz.q: You want three pounds of apples. You say…

quiz.why: The price is for one box.

quiz.q: How do you ask if a seller has strawberries?

pages.title: Reading quest — Saturday at the market · part 1
text: Every Saturday, my friend Lily goes to the farmers market in **San Diego**. The sun is warm, and the fruit is bright. Today I went with her.

We stopped at a table full of apples. “**These apples look good**,” I said. The seller smiled. “**They’re fresh today. Two dollars a pound.**” I said, “**I’ll take three pounds.**” He put the apples on the scale. “**Okay. Anything else?**”

“**Do you have strawberries?**” I asked. “**Yes. Five dollars a box.**” “**One box, please.**” “**That’s eleven dollars**,” he said. I paid, and he said, “**Enjoy your fruit!**” Lily laughed. “**What a steal!**” she said.

fast.why: The writer buys apples and strawberries.

scan.q: How much are the apples per pound?
How many pounds of apples does the writer buy?
How much is the total?

tf.s: The writer goes to a market in San Diego.
tf.why: The first paragraph says this.

tf.s: Strawberries cost two dollars a box.
tf.why: Strawberries are five dollars a box.

tf.s: The seller puts the apples on a scale.
tf.why: He puts them on the scale to weigh them.

tf.s: The writer never wants to go back.
tf.why: They want to go back next Saturday.

pages.title: Reading quest — Saturday at the market · part 2
text: On my way home, I thought about the old rhyme Old Mother Hubbard. She goes to the cupboard to get a bone for her poor dog, but the cupboard is bare. Our bags were full of fruit, so we were lucky. No bare cupboard for us!
At home, I washed the strawberries and put the apples in a bowl. They were sweet and cold. I think I will go back next Saturday. Shopping at a market is slow, friendly and delicious.

pages.title: Reading quest · Talk about it
text: Every Saturday, my friend Lily goes to the farmers market in **San Diego**. The sun is warm, and the fruit is bright. Today I went with her.

We stopped at a table full of apples. “**These apples look good**,” I said. The seller smiled. “**They’re fresh today. Two dollars a pound.**” I said, “**I’ll take three pounds.**” He put the apples on the scale. “**Okay. Anything else?**”

“**Do you have strawberries?**” I asked. “**Yes. Five dollars a box.**” “**One box, please.**” “**That’s eleven dollars**,” he said. I paid, and he said, “**Enjoy your fruit!**” Lily laughed. “**What a steal!**” she said.

On my way home, I thought about the old rhyme Old Mother Hubbard. She goes to the cupboard to get a bone for her poor dog, but the cupboard is bare. Our bags were full of fruit, so we were lucky. No bare cupboard for us!
At home, I washed the strawberries and put the apples in a bowl. They were sweet and cold. I think I will go back next Saturday. Shopping at a market is slow, friendly and delicious.
